_quiz_pool.question: What does c stand for in Q = m × c × ΔT?
_quiz_pool.explanation: c tells how much energy 1 kg needs to warm by 1 °C.

_quiz_pool.question: Which warms fastest with the same energy?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Concrete has a smaller c than water, so its temperature rises more.

_quiz_pool.question: What is the unit of energy Q?
If you double the mass, the energy needed for the same ΔT…
_quiz_pool.explanation: Q grows in step with m.

_quiz_pool.question: Why do parks feel cooler than car parks?
options: Plants and water store heat and evaporate water
_quiz_pool.explanation: Water has a big c and evaporation takes heat away.

_quiz_pool.question: Which roof colour reflects more sunlight?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Light colours reflect more light, so they absorb less energy.

_quiz_pool.question: A city that is warmer than the land around it is called…
_quiz_pool.explanation: Roads and roofs store heat, making an urban heat island.

_quiz_pool.question: Water's specific heat capacity is about…
_quiz_pool.explanation: Water needs about 4,200 J to warm 1 kg by 1 °C.

must_show: two equal cups, one with water and one with sand or soil
both cups in the same sunny spot
a thermometer reading or a hand test before and after 20 minutes
safety: no flame, no kettle, no mains electricity
_lab_rubric.pass_if: The photos show both cups at the start and after 20 minutes, and the student says which warmed more.

cover.fun_fact: Water needs almost 5 times more energy than concrete to warm up by the same amount.
story.title: A hot week in the city
story.lead: Weather forecasters said the coming days would be hot and dry in many cities [1]. Streets and roofs get much hotter than parks [2].
story.image_caption: City surfaces seen in a heat map from space
stat.1.label: joules to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C
stat.2.label: joules to warm 1 kg of concrete by 1 °C
stat.3.label: water needs about 5 times more energy
story.body_1: A city is full of dark roads and concrete roofs. They take in sunlight all day. At night they give the heat back slowly [2]. So a city can stay warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an urban heat island.
story.body_2: Hot days are hard on people, especially older people and babies [3]. Trees, parks and light-coloured roofs help. They reflect sunlight or use it to evaporate water, so less heat is stored [2].
timeline.1.text: The sun starts to warm roads and roofs.
timeline.2.text: Concrete and asphalt are now much hotter than the air.
timeline.3.text: Stored heat flows back out and keeps the city warm.
physics.title: Heat, mass and temperature
physics.body_1: To warm something up you must give it energy. How much depends on three things: how heavy it is, what it is made of, and how much hotter it gets.
physics.body_2: Each material has a specific heat capacity, c. A small c means it heats up quickly. Concrete has a small c. Water has a big c, so it warms slowly.
physics.assumptions: We ignore heat lost to the air and assume all the energy goes into the material.

lab.title: Sun test: sand or water?
lab.step_1: Fill one cup with water and one cup with dry sand or soil.
lab.step_2: Put both cups in the same sunny place for 20 minutes.
lab.step_3: Touch the top of each with a finger or use a thermometer.
lab.question: Which cup got warmer? Use the word c to explain why.
